chapters.title: Chapter 2: Understanding the Asset Classes You're Trading

lessons.title: Alternative and Cross-Border Assets: REITs, InvITs, and International Diversification

body.text: REITs turn rental income into a stock market ticker. InvITs turn a toll road's cash flow into one. Both give a systematic desk exposure to return drivers that have almost nothing to do with corporate earnings or interest rates, at the cost of trading in a market that is nowhere near as deep as the one Nifty 50 futures live in.

children.text: This closes out Chapter 2's asset-by-asset tour with the two categories Chapter 1 flagged but did not detail: exchange-listed alternatives, REITs and InvITs, and cross-border equity exposure accessed from India. Both are genuine diversifiers with return drivers distinct from the four core asset classes. Both also come with real constraints, thin liquidity for the first, a hidden currency bet for the second, that a systematic strategy has to account for rather than assume away.
REITs: Renting Out Commercial Real Estate Through the Stock Market

markDefs.definition: SEBI requires REITs and InvITs to distribute at least 90% of Net Distributable Cash Flows to unit holders, at least semi-annually. This is what makes their yield component comparable to a bond coupon or dividend, rather than being left entirely to management discretion.

children.text: A Real Estate Investment Trust, REIT, holds income-generating commercial property, mainly office parks in India's listed market so far, and passes most of the rental income through to unit holders as a mandated distribution. SEBI requires REITs to distribute
at least 90% of Net Distributable Cash Flows

, so a REIT's return comes from two sources: that distribution yield, and price appreciation or depreciation in the listed units themselves, driven by occupancy rates, rental reversions, and the broader outlook for commercial real estate. India's listed REIT market started with Embassy Office Parks REIT in 2019, followed by Mindspace Business Parks REIT and Brookfield India REIT, all office-focused, and Nexus Select Trust in 2023, India's first retail mall-focused REIT.
InvITs: The Same Idea, Applied to Toll Roads, Power Lines, and Pipelines

Infrastructure Investment Trusts, InvITs, apply the identical structure and the same 90% distribution requirement to infrastructure assets instead of office buildings. India's InvIT market is older than its REIT market, starting with IRB InvIT Fund and IndiGrid in 2017, and now includes names such as PowerGrid InvIT and the NHAI-sponsored National Highways Infra Trust. The underlying cash flow, and therefore the risk, varies meaningfully by what the InvIT actually owns.

body.text: Not all InvIT cash flow is the same kind of "safe." A toll-road InvIT's revenue moves with traffic volume, which can fall in a slowdown. An annuity-based InvIT, where the government pays a fixed sum regardless of traffic, behaves closer to a bond. A power transmission InvIT earns a regulated tariff set by contract, a third distinct risk profile again. Treating "InvIT" as one homogeneous return driver misses exactly the kind of distinction this course keeps insisting matters.

children.text: Why These Are Genuine Diversifiers, and Why They're Thin Markets

Rental income and toll or tariff cash flows respond to occupancy, traffic, and regulated contracts, not to Nifty's earnings cycle or the RBI's rate decisions in any direct sense, which is exactly the kind of genuinely different driver Chapter 1 argued diversification requires. The constraint is size: this is still a small, young market compared to NSE equities, MCX commodities, or G-Secs, with a handful of listed REITs and a modest number of actively traded InvITs, meaningfully lower daily traded volume than any Nifty 50 constituent, and wider spreads that punish a strategy trying to enter or exit quickly at real size.

children.text: International Diversification: What Indian Investors Can Actually Access

RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, LRS, allows a resident individual to remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year abroad, which covers overseas investment among other permitted purposes and is the regulatory ceiling any Indian systematic desk's international allocation has to plan around. In practice, this gets accessed through international investing platforms tied to Indian brokers, giving retail access to US-listed stocks and ETFs, or increasingly through GIFT City, Gujarat's International Financial Services Centre, which offers India-based access to global products under a separate regulatory framework administered by the IFSCA.
Does International Equity Exposure Actually Diversify a Nifty-Heavy Book?

The honest answer is yes, meaningfully, but with real limits Chapter 1's exercise on the S&P 500 already previewed. In calm periods, Indian and US equities respond to different domestic drivers, the RBI versus the Fed, India's domestic consumption cycle versus the US tech and rate cycle, so their correlation runs moderate, not zero, but genuinely below 1. In global systemic shocks, that correlation rises sharply as risk appetite collapses everywhere at once, the same correlation-spike behavior Chapter 1 covered for equities generally. International equity exposure is still equities as an asset class, just a somewhat differently driven slice of it, and it always arrives bundled with the USD-INR currency exposure covered in the previous lesson, whether or not that exposure was deliberately chosen.

children.text: Closing Out the Asset Class Map

Chapter 2 has now covered every asset class this course draws on: equities and their indices, fixed income and the yield curve, commodities and the cost of carry, currencies and covered interest parity, and alternatives and cross-border exposure. Every claim about diversification made so far has been qualitative, driven by different things, correlated differently in crisis versus calm. Chapter 3 turns that into something you can actually measure: correlation matrices, rolling windows, and exactly how much protection each of these asset classes offers, and when.

body.title: The Yield Trade That Couldn't Get Out Fast Enough
body.scenario: A systematic desk adds a small allocation to a listed toll-road InvIT, attracted by its steady distribution yield and low correlation to its other holdings. Three months later, the desk's risk model flags a broad deleveraging event across its book and calls for the InvIT position to be cut by half within a day to meet a firm-wide risk limit. The position proves far harder to exit at a reasonable price than the desk's Nifty futures or G-Sec futures positions did.
body.prompt: What structural feature of this asset class, covered in this lesson, explains why the exit was harder than for the desk's other positions, and what does that imply for how such a position should be sized in the first place?
body.modelAnswer: InvITs, like REITs, trade in a meaningfully thinner, smaller market than NSE equity index futures, G-Sec futures, or MCX commodities, with a modest number of listed names and lower daily traded volume, which means wider spreads and greater price impact when trying to sell a large position quickly. The desk's Nifty and G-Sec futures positions could be unwound near their quoted price because those markets are deep; the InvIT position could not, because the market simply does not have that much daily volume to absorb a large forced sale without moving the price against the seller. The implication for sizing is that a systematic desk should size thin, alternative-asset positions smaller relative to their attractiveness on paper, specifically because of this liquidity constraint, and should not assume it can exit an alternative-asset position on the same timeline or at the same price impact as a core, liquid instrument.

body.title: Reading the Correlation Pattern
body.question: Based on this lesson, how does Nifty 50's correlation to the S&P 500 typically behave across calm periods versus global systemic crises?
options: It stays constant near zero regardless of market conditions
It runs moderate but meaningfully below 1 in calm periods, and rises sharply during global systemic crises
It is always close to 1, since all equity markets move identically
It only correlates during Indian market hours and is unrelated otherwise
body.explanation: International equities offer a genuine, if partial, diversification benefit in calm periods, when Indian and US markets respond to different domestic drivers. That benefit shrinks in global systemic crises, when correlation across equity markets worldwide tends to rise sharply as risk appetite collapses everywhere at once, the same correlation-spike pattern this course has flagged since Chapter 1.

body.title: Naming the Remittance Ceiling
body.textWithBlank: The RBI scheme that allows a resident Indian individual to remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year abroad, covering permitted purposes including overseas investment, is called the ___.
body.explanation: The LRS sets the regulatory ceiling any Indian systematic desk's international allocation has to plan around, since remittances for overseas investment cannot exceed this annual per-individual limit.
